summary: In Greek mythology, Ennomus (Ancient Greek: Ἔννομος) was a Mysian ally of Troy in the Trojan War, son of Arsinous, co-captain with Chromis, and a seer of birds. Homer says that with his auguries he could not ward off black fate: Achilles slew him in the river-melee.

sections.heading: Mysian captain and augur
paragraphs: In the Catalogue of Ships Homer sets Ennomus beside Chromis at the head of the Mysians. He is remembered as a bird-augur, yet the poet foretells that skill in omens will not save him from Achilles' hands in the river where the son of Aeacus made havoc of Trojans and allies alike.
Later, when the fight raged over Patroclus, Hector named Ennomus among the allied captains he heartened — the augur still stood in the battle-din though the Catalogue had already sung his end.

sections.heading: Homonyms
paragraphs: This atlas entry (ennomus-mysian) is the Mysian captain and seer slain by Achilles. Distinct from Ennomus (or Eunomus), a Trojan warrior slain by Odysseus, tracked in the atlas where relevant as a separate Iliadic kill-notice (eunomus-trojan).
